story.title: The Witness Chair, Day Three
story.place: the witness chair in a hearing room
story.goalShort: I want to get through Robb's questioning with my clearance and my word intact.
story.goalFull: I want to get through Robb's questioning with my clearance and my word intact, while he reads from files I have never been allowed to see. I have to answer what I know and not guess.

facts: Garrison asked me whether Frank had been involved in the Chevalier approach.
I said I was very clear on it, that I had a vivid and I thought certainly not fallible memory, and that he had nothing whatever to do with it.
I said it would have been a peculiarly roundabout and unnatural thing, since Chevalier was my friend.
That ended Garrison's direct examination. My lawyers and I thought it had gone well.

Robb got me to agree that close association with the Communist Party was inconsistent with work on a secret war project, then asked about former members. I asked him, "Are we talking about now or then?"
When he asked what test I had applied to my brother, I said, "In the case of a brother you don't make tests, at least I didn't."
I called fellow traveler a repugnant word. I said such a man shouldn't be on a secret war project today, but that during the war it was a question of what the man was like.
He asked if I had ever been one. I said, "I was a fellow traveler," and that I traveled much less fellow after 1939 and very much less after 1942.
Robb reminded me of the Johnson interview. I said that when I was asked why I'd mentioned Eltenton, I invented a cock-and-bull story.
He asked if I told Pash the truth. I said no. He asked if I lied to him. I said yes.
I told him the lie was that Eltenton had tried to approach three members of the project through intermediaries, and that I probably said X had approached three people.
He asked why I did that. I said, "Because I was an idiot."

Robb read me extracts from the 1943 Pash transcript. I didn't recall saying them but wouldn't deny it. He said, "Doctor, for your information, I might say we have a record of your voice." I said, "Sure."
He took me through the consulate, the microfilm and the other contacts. I said, "This whole thing was a pure fabrication except for the one name Eltenton."
Garrison asked Gray whether we could be given a copy of the transcript as Robb read from it. Gray and Robb agreed a classification officer might decide that at the end of the day.
Robb went back to reading. At the end he asked if I had told Pash a whole fabrication and tissue of lies. I said, "Right."
Robb said my acquaintance with Jean was fairly casual. I said our meetings were rare but that there was still very deep feeling when we saw each other.
He asked why I had to see her in 1943. I said, "Because she was still in love with me," and that she took me to the airport and I never saw her again.
He asked if I spent the night with her. I said yes, that it was not good practice, and when he asked how I knew she wasn't dangerous, I said, "I knew her."
He had me name her friends and say which were Communists. I gave him the names and asked, "Is the list long enough?"

steps.title: Clear Frank

steps.userSide: Your Step: the second part of your Goal.

steps.title: Answer for Jean

voice: Short, plain sentences. Most spoken sentences are under 12 words.
Concrete things (a glass of water, a microphone, a chair, a clock), not abstractions.
Dry one-line wit now and then, never for effect. No grand sentences, no moral.
Say what he feels directly (tired, wary, impatient) and what is in front of him.
He answers exactly, in complete sentences, and does not guess at what he cannot remember.
Under pressure he becomes more formal, not less.

card_why: I want every answer to be one I can stand behind tomorrow. A careless word is easy to say and hard to take back.
card_now: A glass of water sits on the ledge in front of me. I turn it a quarter turn and look at the room.
card_feeling: I am tense, and I notice it in the grip of my hand on the chair arm. The room is warm and nobody is in a hurry.
